title: Police commander defends decision to breach bedroom door
subtitle: Joshua Megeney was fatally shot by police three minutes after Sgt. Ken Kane used a ram to smash open the door separating them.
article: Joshua John Robert Kyle Megeney's family members sobbed quietly as the province's chief forensic pathologist described in clinical detail how the .223-calibre round from a Saskatoon police officer's rifle killed him.

"He would have been unconscious and dropped to the ground," Shaun Ladham said of the moment the bullet entered the forehead of the 28-year-old man from Medicine Hat, Alta., during a standoff on Oct. 6, 2018.

"There would be no recovery from this. I would think that it would have been instantaneous," Ladham said of the wound sustained during what has been characterized as a "suicide or death by cop scenario."

Megeney's death in the upstairs bedroom of an Avenue Q North home following reports of a break-and-enter in progress is the subject of a coroner's inquest at Saskatoon Court of Queen's Bench this week.

Inquests are intended to establish the cause of death and set out recommendations to prevent similar deaths in the future. While the six-member jury is not tasked with assigning blame, the proceeding has nevertheless been combative.

That was evident Thursday morning when Saskatoon city police Sgt. Ken Kane, who led the team of tactical support unit officers into the house that day, testified about his decision to breach a door moments before gunshots rang out.

At the time, Megeney was in a bedroom with three loaded hunting rifles, including a high-powered 7mm Remington Magnum. The inquest heard he refused to come out despite repeated verbal commands from police.

Three minutes after Kane used a ram to smash the door open between six and 12 inches, Const. Blake Atkinson and Const. Jesse Jackson fired three rounds at Megeney, who, they told the inquest, pointed the 7mm rifle at them.
One of the bullets, believed to be from Jackson's police-issued semi-automatic rifle, struck Megeney in the middle of his forehead.

Kane testified that he decided to breach the door to open up lines of communication with the then-unknown suspect, both for officers on the scene and for crisis negotiators who were on their way. Attempts to talk through the door were unsuccessful, he said.

The 22-year police force veteran went on to say that, in his experience, suspects often give up after the last barrier between them and police officers is removed, but that he never would have proceeded if he knew Megeney had rifles.

"If I had known for a second what was going on in there, I never would have made entry into the residence," Kane said of the bedroom, which he believed at the time contained hunting rifles in a locked and inaccessible gun safe.

Under cross-examination by Scott Spencer, the lawyer representing Megeney's family, Kane was questioned repeatedly about his decision to breach the door before negotiators arrived and why other means of communication weren't attempted.

Kane said using a ladder or other means, such as the police force's "Bearcat" armoured vehicle, to look in the bedroom window would have left officers too exposed, and that it would not have been feasible to slide a cellphone under the bedroom door.

While there was "no urgency" to breach the door, it was important to establish a clear line of communication, Kane testified, adding that it did not cross his mind that the break-and-enter suspect might be under the influence of drugs.

Ladham testified that he found a "high level" of methamphetamine, enough to potentially kill a user without a high tolerance for the drug, in Megeney's blood and signs of intravenous drug use on his arms.

At one point, Crown prosecutor Robin Ritter - who is serving as coroner's counsel during the inquest - rose to suggest that Spencer's questions had been repeatedly asked and answered. The same pattern has played out repeatedly this week.
"This is far, far out of control," lawyer Alma Wiebe, the presiding coroner, was forced to interject during an even more heated exchange on Wednesday, the inquest's third full day of testimony.
Thursday was the inquest's final day of evidence. The four women and two men on the jury are expected to begin their deliberations at 9:30 a.m. on Friday.
